subject: gunblade
pitch:
Category: Weapon.
Subject: gunblade.
Style: Final Fantasy.

spec.name: Gunblade of the Lion Knight
spec.description: A Final Fantasy style gunblade: an oversized broad sword whose guard and ricasso hold a revolver chamber, trigger and grip, with gold filigree, a lion emblem and glowing cyan crystal accents.
spec.layout: Vertical display pose, blade up (+Y), flat faces toward +Z/-Z, centred on x=0, standing on y=0 with the pommel tip on the floor (a prop). From bottom to top: pommel with a tassel (y 0 to 0.1), grip wrapped in leather (0.1 to 0.34) with a trigger guard and trigger on the +Z side of the blade-side edge, then the revolver mechanism (hammer, a six-chamber cylinder and a short barrel, y 0.34 to 0.56) that sits between a bold winged crossguard and the blade root, then a long single-edged blade (0.56 to 1.35) with a thick spine at -X, a bevelled edge at +X, a fuller groove, a notched tip and an angled clipped point. Colours go by place: steel blade with a pale edge highlight, dark gunmetal mechanism, gold trim on every edge, deep blue leather and cloth, a red gem and cyan glowing runes. Bold chunky shapes, FF style: oversized and ornate, a lion emblem repeated on the guard, blade root and pommel.

parts.builds: The main blade from bladeRoot to the tip: thick steel slab with spine on -X and a lighter bevelled edge strip on +X, a recessed fuller groove with cyan rune glyphs, gold inlay lines along the spine, a notched step near the tip, a clipped angled point, edge highlight strip in steelEdge, a gold lion emblem plate at the root and small dark outline strips.
parts.attaches: Root sits on guardCenter/bladeRoot and overlaps into the guard slightly.

parts.builds: The ornate crossguard at guardCenter: a gold chunky central block, two swept wing prongs (left longer, curved up) with goldDark undersides, a red gem in the middle ringed in gold, a lion head emblem relief, small studs, blue cloth ribbon pieces tied at the sides, and the ricasso collar where the blade enters.
parts.attaches: Blade root enters above at bladeRoot; the mechanism's top barrel sits flush under it at y 0.56.

parts.builds: The revolver assembly between grip and guard (y 0.34 to 0.56): gunmetal frame block, a six-chamber cylinder with brass bullet tips and flutes, a short barrel with muzzle ring along the blade's spine, a hammer, a rear sight, gold screws and rivets, cyan glowing core lines, and a trigger guard loop with a trigger on the +Z side.
parts.attaches: Bottom meets the grip at gripTop; top meets the guard at guardCenter.

parts.builds: Grip and pommel from the floor to gripTop: a leather grip with diagonal wrap strips in leather and leatherDark, gold ferrule rings at both ends, a faceted gold pommel with a lion emblem and a cyan crystal cap, a red cloth tassel with gold bead hanging from a ring on the pommel and falling to the floor side, tiny rivets.
parts.attaches: Top at gripTop meets the mechanism; the pommel base touches y=0.

calls.reasoning:
I'm planning the buildHilt function, noting there are no joints in this model so geometry stays in model space using b.part with position only. I'll leave the Ctx type as-is, assuming it's provided globally by the module rather than needing an import.

Now I'm working out the hilt's dimensions: a narrow box shape for the grip, with a faceted gold pommel touching the floor at the bottom, topped by a cyan crystal cap, and I'm iterating on where exactly to place the crystal relative to the pommel's lathe-shaped body.

I'm also planning a lion emblem for the pommel's front face, assembled from simple primitives — a dark backing disc, a ring of small cones for the mane, a sphere for the face, and basic shapes for eyes, nose, and ears, built as a reusable helper that can mirror to either side.

For the tassel, I'm attaching a small torus ring to the spine side of the pommel near the floor, with a cord hanging down to a gold bead and then a cloth skirt of strands, keeping everything compact within the bounding box so it drapes naturally toward the ground.

Adjusting tassel bead radius so it fits within the box bounds, confirming floor contact works out. Now I'm sizing the grip as an octagonal cylinder in leather tones, slightly elongated to fit the blade attachment point, and thinking through how to add diagonal wrap strips, possibly via a helical sweep.

I'll make the base cylinder leatherDark with lighter leather wrap strips swept in low-poly helices, then add gold ferrules with flared lathe profiles at the grip ends, plus small gold rivet spheres ringed around the ferrules at the wrap crossings.

Since there's no joint hierarchy needed for static parts, I'll place the rings using plain loops with cosine-based positioning rather than bone frames, keeping it simple and safe. For the pommel I'm lathing a rounded gold profile outline around the y-axis to cap the grip.

Adding a darker gold ring band near the top of the pommel for contrast, plus small studs around its base, then capping it with a crystal built from a scaled octahedron sitting just above the pommel's peak.

I'm pulling in a glow effect from the kit and scattering four tiny octahedron shards around the crystal's collar as accent facets, using a lighter cyan tone for a subtle highlight against the main rune cyan.

Now I'm working out the ferrules: a bottom flared gold ferrule and a top flush ferrule with a dark gold ring detail, and considering adding small rivet spheres around the bottom ferrule using the darker gold tone for texture.

For the pommel, I'm placing a lion emblem as a dark gold disc on its front facet, accounting for the octagonal pommel's curved vs. flat vertex geometry so the plate sits flush against the correct surface radius rather than floating or clipping through it.

Now I'm designing the lion itself: a mane made from eight small cones arranged radially like rays, a gold face sphere, tiny ink spheres for eyes and nose, and small sphere ears, wrapped into a reusable lion() helper function that takes position, scale, and facing direction.

Adjusting tassel positioning...

Adjusting strand geometry to taper and flare outward like a real tassel...

Laying out the tassel sequence top to bottom: ring, cord, gold bead, cord, neck cap, cloth head sphere, then skirt strands trailing down. For the pommel I'm skipping ornate vertex-aligned facet strips and going simpler with gold-dark ring bands and studs instead.

For the grip I'm keeping the cross-section circular rather than oval for consistency, sizing the base cylinder and planning four helical strands wrapping around it -- two leather strands in a counter-helix pattern plus a thin gold thread helix offset to sit between them.

Writing strand sweep code...

Still working out the lion geometry...

Now I'm tallying up the total part count to make sure I stay under budget: lion face details (backing, rim, mane, disc, ears, eyes, nose, muzzle) come to about 21 per side, doubled to 42, plus pommel body, ring band, and studs adding roughly 10 more.

Adding the crystal, lug/ring, tassel cord, bead, strands, grip sweeps, and ferrule rivets, I land around 99 parts total, which gives me comfortable headroom. I'm planning out the rivet placement on the ferrules using angular positions around the cylinder.

Placing rivets near the bottom ferrule edge, then working out gold band positions for the pommel and small studs along the grip's tapered profile, estimating radii at specific heights to keep everything aligned with the handle's curve.

Realizing the front-facing studs would collide with the emblem placement, I'm shifting the emblem scale down slightly and skipping studs at the angles directly facing front/back, using six studs spaced at 45-degree offsets instead of eight. Time to write the code for this.

I'll write buildMechanism using the provided Ctx type without importing it, keeping parts in model space since there are no joints. I'm placing the blade with spine at the negative x side and edge at the positive x side.

For the revolver mechanism box, I'm figuring out the layout: a vertical cylinder (axis along y, matching the blade/barrel direction) sits near the hilt, sized to fit within the z-depth constraints, with a gunmetal frame block below it and a hammer positioned toward the spine side.

Now I'm placing the trigger guard - since the trigger sits on the edge side of the blade, I'm positioning the guard loop near x≈0.05-0.06, projecting toward +z, as a curved sweep spanning roughly y 0.34-0.45, trying to work out whether it should lie in the YZ plane or the XY plane for the most natural gunblade look.

For the hammer, I'm considering placement at the spine side near the top of the frame, but reconsidering since on a barrel-up design the rear of the cylinder actually corresponds to the grip end rather than the top.

Positioning the barrel to overlap the cylinder top near the guard, flush at 0.56 with a gold muzzle ring, and considering shifting it toward the spine side with a rib detail for visual interest.

Now I'm placing the front sight on the barrel and figuring out the rear sight location — deciding to notch it onto the frame near the spine edge below the cylinder. I'm also laying out the lower frame as a box and adding thin side plates to shroud the cylinder.

Actually, I'm reconsidering: instead of hiding the cylinder with side plates, I'll leave it exposed with a back strap and front strap post on either side, plus upper and lower frame collars, while working out exact box dimensions and positions for the posts, top strap, and cylinder itself.

Now I'm detailing the cylinder geometry with flat segments and gunmetal material, adding six dark flute grooves around its circumference, and planning brass bullet tips poking up from the top face at six radial positions.

Sizing the bullet cones so their tips peek above the cylinder's top ring, then adding cyan glow accents—thin strips on the post faces and a subtle glowing ring torus around the cylinder—using the glow kit for that neon highlight effect.

Now I'm detailing the cylinder itself: gold bands at the top and bottom edges, and dark flute cutouts between the chambers positioned radially around the outside, giving it that authentic revolver texture.

Then I'm adding hardware accents — small gold screws with slotted heads on the frame's side faces, oriented along the correct axis, plus tiny gold rivets on the top strap and lower block corners for added realism.

I'm also working out the lower block geometry: sizing its width and depth, adding a slightly larger gold collar band near the top, and planning a chamfered top edge along with thin gold trim strips along the vertical edges.

Now I'm figuring out where to position the hammer piece relative to the lower block, trying to keep it within the block's boundaries while deciding whether it should protrude outward or sit on the top yoke instead.

Plotting hammer outline coordinates...

I'll skip the fine serration detail and just give the hammer a steel highlight with a gold pin, using gunmetalLight against the darker frame. For the rear plates I'm positioning boxes near x=-0.052 spanning y 0.405-0.505 with z offsets around ±0.032, and adding a solid front post at x=0.058 before working out where the trigger guard sits on the +Z side.

Now I'm plotting the trigger guard loop as a path in the YZ plane at x=0.058, tracing points outward from the lower block face (around y=0.455, z=0.03) through an arc to y=0.425, z=0.06 and back down to embed into the block near y=0.35-0.38, making sure both ends anchor properly into the block/post geometry since the block only reaches z=0.045.

Now I'm shaping the trigger as a small curved extrusion in the YZ plane near the guard, giving it a gold finish to match the trim, defining its outline with a short sequence of points that curve down and back to form the trigger shape.

Next I'm positioning the barrel as a cylinder offset from the yoke box, placing it above the yoke which sits in its own region of the frame.

I'm angling it along the blade's spine, adding a gold muzzle ring, a rib on the far side, an underbarrel lug, a small front sight wedge, and a bore disc at the muzzle tip to finish the geometry.

Realizing the barrel's offset x doesn't line up with the cylinder's center, I'm reconsidering and deciding to center both at x=0 for consistency, keeping the yoke and rear sight placement centered along the spine too.

Now I'm shortening the barrel to a stubby 0.03 length sitting right above the yoke, and adding small wedge-shaped side flanges along it for detail, topped with a gold accent. I'm also sketching in thin glowing cyan strips on the yoke's front faces and considering vertical cyan accents on the front sight post.

Then I'm adding more cyan lines on the lower block faces, plus a thin glowing torus ring around the cylinder, and thinking through small gold corner trim pieces on the lower block and yoke top edges. I'm also starting to plan a notched rear sight block on the yoke.

Adjusting the cylinder-rod layering...

I'll keep a gold collar under the guard and add thin cyan accent lines along the barrel flanks, skipping the brass casing detail, while staying within the six-color limit. I'm setting up helper functions for boxes and cylinders with flat shading, with cylinders oriented along the z-axis, then wrapping relevant parts in a glow effect.

Now I'm working out the cylinder chamber flutes, skipping the ratchet teeth, and aligning the flutes radially with the six bullet positions at 60-degree intervals, sizing them as thin dark boxes that protrude slightly beyond the cylinder's 12-gon surface.

Adding gold trim bands near the top and bottom of the yoke, plus small rivet spheres at the yoke corners and screw cylinders on the lower block faces to add mechanical detail.

Also placing a gold pivot pin through the hammer with end caps, and considering minor accent touches like an ink underline recess and a ledge detail, though I'll keep these minimal to avoid overcomplicating the model.

Now I'm figuring out where to add cyan accent lines -- deciding the front post area is too cramped with the trigger guard overlap, so I'll place the cyan strips on the yoke, lower block, and ring instead, finalizing the part placement toward roughly 100 pieces before writing the code.

I'm figuring out how to type the buildGuard function's parameter against the module-provided Ctx type without causing a naming conflict, considering whether a local type alias would shadow it safely within this module's scope.

Now I'm designing the sword guard geometry: a centered box at y=0.56 with the blade passing through it, a collar fitted above where it's slightly wider than the blade, and asymmetric wings extending from the central block—one longer and curved upward on one side, the other shorter—built using an extrusion technique from an outline in the X-Y plane.

Checking the wing outline's max x extent, I realize it overshoots the bounding box, so I'm shrinking the base point and scaling the points down to fit within 0.17.

For the right wing, I'm mirroring the shape but making it shorter with a reduced curve, then working out a thin underside strip of gold detail beneath the outline.

Tracing dark trim outline points...

I'll make this dark layer slightly thicker than the gold base so it peeks out as a visible trim edge, then consider adding small gold studs on the wing front faces for extra detail.

Adjusting coordinates...

Adding more geometry blocks...

I'm checking that the mechanism barrel fits within the block's footprint. For the front face, I'm planning a red gem ringed with gold sitting on the central block, using a scaled octahedron for the gem and a low-poly torus for the ring, mirrored on the back face, plus considering a lion head relief on the block.

I'll settle on placing the lion head medallion on the front, with the gem embedded as the forehead jewel at its center -- building it as a dark disc backing, gold mane spikes, face features, and the red gem nested within.

I'll simplify: front gets the gem ringed with a radiating gold sunburst mane, back gets the full lion head. I'm writing a helper to build the lion geometry oriented along the z-axis so it can be placed on either face.

Adding the lion head details...

Continuing the medallion design... for the inner mane disc, face shape, and small goldDark features like eyes, nose, muzzle, and brow ridge. For the front side I'm laying out a central gem on a torus ring, a twelve-spike sunburst mane alternating long and short spikes, and a backing disc for depth.

I'm reusing the sunburst function for both front and back, placing gold stud spheres at the block corners, and considering whether to add a tiny cyan accent line since the spec mentions runes elsewhere but no major cyan element is needed here.

I decide to add small cyan glowing bead accents on the wing inlays using the glow kit, positioning them at the inlay z-depth near the inner wing area.

Now I'm designing the blue cloth ribbon ties: wrapping leather bands around each wing base with gold knot spheres, then adding hanging tail sweeps from the knots using catmull paths for a draped effect.

Defining the tail notch points...

Adjusting tail lengths to hang just below the wing without overlapping the mechanism, positioning two angled tail pieces per side in front for a flared tie look, with knots front-only but tails on both sides. Now considering an asymmetric mirror where the left wing is slightly longer than the right.

Deciding to skip the extra prongs and highlights for simplicity, but adding a ricasso collar with gold and dark gold bands near the blade's base, considering small ornamental touches like gold wedges or spheres before settling on a simpler collar design.

Still placing block geometry...

Calculating wing tip placement...

Checking the scaled inner points against the right outer boundary at several x-values to confirm they stay within bounds, then working out the world-space placement formula for extras by mirroring the x-coordinate for the right side.

Now I'm writing a helper function to place decorative parts without bone attachments, and sketching out a sunburst pattern made of alternating cones radiating outward plus a central disc, assigning colors and positioning them around the piece.

Still placing decorative elements...

Calculating facial feature positions...

Now I'm working out the wing's inlay placement, stud and bead positions on both faces, then setting up the extrusion call with typed outline points for the wing geometry.

For the smoothing, I'm reasoning through whether rounding corners at 1x quarter-length could cause the cuts to overlap on short edges — concluding it's safe since the quarter-cuts from each end never exceed half the edge length. Now I'm thinking through the tail extrusion setup, considering tilt via the y-axis vector relative to the default upward orientation.

Then I'm working out tail positions and knot details — placing leather octahedron knots at each side with small spheres, and wondering whether to add a gold bead accent on top of each knot. For the extrusion direction, I'm noting the y-vector used for tilt isn't actually perpendicular to x, so I'm considering whether the renderer auto-orthogonalizes these axes via cross product before computing thickness.

Still refining the ribbon geometry: adjusting the hanging outline length so the bottom edge lands just under the midline, checking tail symmetry by mirroring knots to the back side, and sketching out box dimensions for the band and a thin gold edge strip along its lower border.

Now I'm finalizing the band's vertical bounds so the gold trim sits flush at the top and bottom edges without poking through the wing geometry. I'm also setting up the glow import path and planning the `mk` helper along with rotation conventions for cylinder parts pointing along z.

I'm drafting the buildBlade function, relying on the module-provided Ctx type without importing it, and since there are no joints I can skip bone setup and just place parts directly using geometry, color, and position.

Now I'm sketching out the blade geometry as an extruded outline in the x-y plane: a thin slab with the spine on the -X side, the edge on +X, and a notch partway up before an angled clip leading to the tip, aiming for that classic gunblade silhouette with a stepped spine and diagonal point.

Still plotting outline coordinates...

Simplifying the bevel approach...

I think I'll shrink the main slab slightly short of the tip, then overlay a separate tapering wedge prism at the very edge so it reads as a distinct beveled cutting edge rather than being buried inside the slab's surface.

Actually, maybe a simpler approach: instead of hand-building a wedge, I could just apply a uniform bevel to the whole slab outline using a small chamfer radius, which would naturally round the tip along with the rest of the edge.

Simplifying the approach: I'll just use a single lighter steelEdge strip over the bevel region with matching chamfer, accepting slight overlap rather than overengineering separate thickness offsets.

Adjusting thickness and bevel values so the slab and strip don't clash geometrically, then thinking about how to fake a recessed fuller groove since the slab can't actually be cut — maybe using darker inset strips or thinning the slab in that region instead.

Since extrude can't handle holes directly, I realize I should split the raised layer into separate pieces instead: one for the spine side, one for the edge side, plus a top cap and bottom cap joining above and below the groove, each extruded separately at the same thickness, with the groove floor formed by the core slab underneath.

But I'm now worried about seams -- bevels on the interior edges where these pieces join (like where the spine piece meets the cap at the groove's end) would create visible V-shaped notches instead of a clean surface. I'm reconsidering whether to treat the raised area as a single C-shaped outline instead, connecting the groove to the outer edge through a thin slit so it stays one continuous non-self-intersecting polygon.

Since the bottom of the blade near y=0.56 is hidden under the guard collar, I can let the groove's slit open there without it being visible, which simplifies the shape into one polygon: I'm working out the exact coordinates tracing the outer outline up one side, around the pointed groove tip near the top, and back down the other side to close the slit at the bottom.

Defining edge strip coordinates...

Checking that the inner point stays within the edge boundary confirms the offset is valid. I'm also adjusting the strip thickness and bevel slightly to avoid z-fighting with the raised surface, nudging the height up a fraction of a millimeter while keeping it within bounds.

Now I'm working out the spine bar geometry on the -X side, defining its thickness and outline points so it aligns correctly with the notch in the raised outline near the top.

Adding thin gold inlay lines near the spine edges, then defining a recessed groove with its own slightly different slate tone, and laying out the core outline polygon coordinates for the book's main shape.

For the groove itself I'm keeping it thin with no bevel since the raised outer layers will cover the edges, then placing glowing cyan rune glyphs along the groove floor using the glow kit, building each rune from a couple thin bar strips arranged vertically.

Adding subtle outline strips along the groove edges and spine for extra definition, though keeping it minimal since the bevel already does most of the visual work.

Now I'm thinking about the notch detail near the spine—adding a small gold accent strip along the diagonal cut, a steel highlight along the clipped edge for a beveled look, and a few cyan rune dots nearby for accent.

Then I'm considering a lion emblem gold plate near the blade root, positioned just below the guard collar over the groove area, sizing it as a shield-like outline wider than the groove itself so it sits visibly on the blade face.

Now I'm designing a simplified lion face relief on the plate using goldDark and ink accents — a circular head with a mane ring of triangular spikes, ears, eyes, nose, and muzzle positioned at the plate's center with a helper function to place parts symmetrically on both faces.

Working out the mirroring math...

Since the lion head is symmetric, I'll use symmetric vertex sets so the mirror logic doesn't matter, and extrude thickness centered at the given z position. For the lion head front view I'm planning the mane as a 12-point star outline extruded in dark gold, then adding a lighter gold face disk approximated as an octagon on top.

Continuing the layered build: ears as small gold octagons placed near the top, slanted ink boxes for eyes over the face, a pale gold octagon muzzle, and an ink triangle for the nose.

Still layering coordinates...

I'm checking whether the plate fully covers the groove slit at each y-level, and noting that near the shield's tapered tip the plate narrows enough that the groove becomes visible again at the bottom.

I'm thinking about decorating the groove near its endpoint: maybe a small gold cap around y 1.17-1.2, a glowing cyan diamond at the tip, and a sequence of runes placed along the groove between y 0.80 and 1.13.

Laying out rune positions and glyph templates...

Totaling things up, I'm estimating around 110 parts counting gold trim, ink lines, shield plates, lions, and runes. I'm also planning additional gold inlay strips along the spine bar's top and side faces for extra detail.

Positioning the gold inlay and ink lines on the spine bar's top face, adjusting thin box dimensions so they sit flush without poking through the bevel edges.

Placing gold coordinates for notch...

Now I'm adding thin ink outline strips along the groove edges to darken the transitions where the bevel meets the raised faces and floor.

Adding small gold studs to the plate corners, then double-checking the layered thicknesses so the gold and lion elements stay within the 0.025 z-limit without clipping through the raised layer.

Working out the lion's layered thicknesses for star, disc, and feature extrusions so they stack cleanly within the base height, and centering each part's z-offset by half its thickness. Since this is a static model with no joints, I'll skip passing a bone reference and just let the geometry build directly in model space.

Now I'm checking the extrude outline requirements and verifying the raised layer sits centered at z=0 using the standard x-axis orientation, while confirming the narrow slit geometry and its bevel width won't cause issues at the concave corners.

I'm working out the edge strip polygon coordinates, adjusting the bottom start point to align with the raised layer and guard collar so the bevel stays hidden, then checking whether the point ordering keeps the shape consistent.

I'm adding a glow effect using the glow helper on flat-colored parts, plus a small octahedron gem accent at the groove top. I'm also setting up gold inlay lines and edge studs, plus the repeated lion emblem, then starting on shared helper constants for the side arrangement.

Writing box and segment helper functions...

Now I'm designing the lion emblem geometry — a 24-point alternating star for the mane, octagon disc for the face, scaled ellipse for the muzzle, and small hexagons for the ears, all positioned relative to the shield plate's center.

Working out the layering for muzzle, nose, mouth, and eyes, stacking z-thicknesses so each feature sits just above the one below without clipping. For the eyes I'm planning slanted rectangles via rotated boxes to get a slight angled look.

Adding brows and nose as a small triangular extrusion, with the mouth built from a vertical box plus curved side pieces. I'm also checking that the symmetry holds correctly between front and back faces, making sure paired features at mirrored x-positions use opposite rotation signs so the emblem stays visually symmetric in world space.

Now I'm defining glyph templates for the rune designs using normalized coordinate sets that get scaled down to fit the emblem, building out a few different shapes like a T-form, a diamond, and others as line segments...

I'm placing the seven glyphs in a vertical sequence with evenly spaced positions, checking that each glyph's top edge stays clear of the groove line above it, then setting a floor depth for the engraving.

Now I'm working out the thin cyan edge-strip positions that frame the groove, making sure their spacing leaves enough clearance around the glyphs' width, and placing matching ink outline strokes inside the groove walls that stop short of the slanted top edge.

I'm defining the material palette next—steel, steel edge, spine, and gold tones—then checking for z-fighting between the core slit and raised surfaces. With the blade tip's clipped angle confirmed and the guard finalized, I'm turning to the lion plate shield, setting up its outline coordinates and extrusion parameters relative to the center position.

Now I'm writing the extrusion helper with bevel support for the plate outlines, setting up TypeScript types for outline points that can include sharp corner markers, then placing gold studs around the plate's inner corners near the top edge.

Finally I'm writing the exported buildBlade function that destructures only the context pieces it needs, ignoring unused ones, and pulling steel material from the P parameter.
